title: Numbers, age, and telling time
objectives: Count from 1 to 100 using native Tagalog numbers
Recognize and use the Spanish-derived numbers for time and everyday counting
Say your age and ask someone else's
Tell the time with alas- and ask Anong oras na?
Use classroom survival phrases: paki-, hindi ko maintindihan

grammar.title: Native numbers 1 to 100
grammar.explanation:
The native Tagalog numbers 1–10 are: isa, dalawa, tatlo, apat, lima, anim, pito, walo, siyam, sampu. Learn these ten cold — everything else is built from them.

The teens add labing- in front: labing-isa (11), labindalawa (12), labintatlo (13) ... labinsiyam (19). (The spelling shifts slightly: labing- before vowels and l/w, labin- before d/t/s.)

Tens use -mpu: dalawampu (20), tatlumpu (30), apatnapu (40), limampu (50), animnapu (60), pitumpu (70), walumpu (80), siyamnapu (90), and sandaan or isang daan (100). To combine tens and ones, join them with 't (a shortened at, 'and'): dalawampu't isa (21), limampu't lima (55).

When a number describes a noun, it takes the little linker -ng or na: isang guro (one teacher), dalawang estudyante (two students), sampung taon (ten years). For now just copy this pattern — the linker gets its own lesson in Unit 5.

grammar.title: Spanish numbers — and when Filipinos use which set
grammar.explanation:
Because of 300 years of Spanish rule, Tagalog has a second, Spanish-derived number set: uno, dos, tres, kuwatro, singko, sais, siyete, otso, nuwebe, diyes. Real Manila speech mixes the two sets by habit, not by rule of grammar but by topic.

Use the SPANISH set for: clock time (alas-dos = two o'clock), prices in the market (dose pesos is heard alongside labindalawang piso), and often for age in casual speech.

Use the NATIVE set for: counting objects (tatlong mansanas), and in more formal or written Tagalog.

You don't have to master big Spanish numbers at this level — but you must recognize uno to diyes, plus dose (12), because clocks only go to twelve.

examples.en: one, two, three, four, five (Spanish set)

examples.tl: sais, siyete, otso, nuwebe, diyes, onse, dose
examples.en: six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve (Spanish set)

grammar.title: Telling time with alas-
grammar.explanation:
Clock time uses alas- plus a Spanish number: alas-dos (2 o'clock), alas-otso (8 o'clock). One o'clock is special: ala-una (from Spanish 'a la una').

To ask the time: Anong oras na? — 'What time is it (already)?' The particle na means 'already/now' and is almost always included. A typical answer: Alas-tres na po — 'It's three o'clock.'

To say morning/afternoon/evening, add ng + part of day: alas-otso ng umaga (8 a.m.), ala-una ng hapon (1 p.m.), alas-siyete ng gabi (7 p.m.). Half past uses y medya: alas-dos y medya (2:30).

Don't translate 'it is' — Tagalog just states the time: Alas-dos na. Literally 'Two o'clock already.'

grammar.title: Survival phrases: paki- requests and 'I don't understand'
grammar.explanation:
Stick paki- in front of an action word and you get a polite request — Tagalog's built-in 'please': pakiulit (please repeat), pakibagal (please slow down). Add po and lang ('just') to soften further: Pakiulit po. Pakibagalan lang po.

The most important learner sentence in this whole course is Hindi ko maintindihan — 'I don't understand.' Learn it as a fixed chunk; the word ko means 'I/my' in a second pronoun set you'll study properly in Unit 4.

Its partners: Hindi ko alam — 'I don't know', and Sandali lang po — 'Just a moment, please.' With these plus pakiulit, you can survive any conversation that runs ahead of you.

example.en: There are seven of us at home.

example.tl: Walong taon na ang kapatid ko.
example.en: My sibling is eight years old.
I was ten years old then.

vocab.note: Tens end in -mpu/-napu: tatlumpu 30, apatnapu 40, limampu 50
't joins tens and ones: limampu't lima = 55

example.en: There are a hundred students at the school.

vocab.note: Then onse 11, dose 12 — clocks stop at dose

vocab.note: Literally 'how many years are you already?'

example.tl: Ilang taon ka na? — Labing-walong taon na ako.
example.en: How old are you? — I'm eighteen.

example.tl: Pasensya na po, hindi ko po maintindihan.

dialogue.title: In Tagalog class
dialogue.context: Kate, an American student, is in her first Tagalog class with Teacher Reyes.

lines.speaker: G. Reyes
lines.tl: Magandang umaga sa inyong lahat! Kumusta kayo?
lines.en: Good morning, everyone! How are you all?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Magandang umaga po! Mabuti naman po.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Pakiulit po. Hindi ko po maintindihan.
lines.en: Please repeat that. I don't understand.

lines.speaker: G. Reyes
lines.tl: Sige. I-lang ta-on ka na? Mabagal, ha.
lines.en: Okay. How - old - are - you? Slowly, alright.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Ah! Dalawampu't isang taon na po ako.

lines.speaker: G. Reyes
lines.en: Good! What time is it, Kate?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Sandali lang po... Alas-nuwebe y medya na po ng umaga.
lines.en: Just a moment... It's nine thirty in the morning.

lines.speaker: G. Reyes
lines.tl: Tama! At anong oras na sa Amerika?
lines.en: Correct! And what time is it in America?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Hindi ko po alam! Alas-nuwebe ng gabi?
lines.en: I don't know! Nine in the evening?

lines.speaker: G. Reyes
lines.en: Yes, correct. Thank you very much, Kate.

exercises.prompt: What is 'five' in the native Tagalog number set?
exercises.explain: Lima is native Tagalog; singko is the Spanish-derived word for five, used mainly for time and prices.

exercises.prompt: Which number set do Filipinos use for clock time?
exercises.explain: Clock time always uses the Spanish set with alas-: alas-dos, alas-tres, and so on.
Sampu is ten; the teens then build on it with labing-: labing-isa, labindalawa...
Tens and ones are joined with 't (short for at, 'and'): dalawampu't isa.

exercises.prompt: Anong oras na? (It's 3 o'clock.) — ___-tres na po.
exercises.explain: Clock hours take alas- plus the Spanish number: alas-tres. Only one o'clock differs: ala-una.

exercises.tl: Alas-otso y medya na ng umaga.
exercises.explain: Alas-otso is eight o'clock, y medya adds the half hour, and ng umaga places it in the morning.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: Ilang taon ka na? What do they want to know?
exercises.explain: Ilang taon ka na? is literally 'how many years are you already?' — the standard way to ask age.

exercises.prompt: You are 25. Complete: Dalawampu't limang ___ na ako.
exercises.explain: Age is stated as number + taon (years) + na: Dalawampu't limang taon na ako.

exercises.prompt: Please repeat that. I don't understand. (polite)
exercises.answer: Pakiulit po. Hindi ko po maintindihan.
accept: Pakiulit po. Hindi ko po maintindihan
Pakiulit po, hindi ko po maintindihan
exercises.explain: Paki- turns ulit (repeat) into a polite request, and Hindi ko maintindihan is the set phrase for 'I don't understand'.

exercises.tl: Ilang taon ka na? — Labing-walong taon na po ako.
exercises.prompt: How old is the person answering?
exercises.explain: Labing-walo is 18 (labing- + walo, eight). The answer means 'I'm eighteen years old.'

exercises.prompt: Anong oras na po? — Ala-una na po ng hapon.
exercises.answer: What time is it? — It's one in the afternoon.
accept: What time is it? It's one in the afternoon
What time is it? It is one o'clock in the afternoon
What time is it? It's 1 p.m.
What time is it? It's one pm
exercises.explain: Ala-una (not alas-una) is one o'clock, and ng hapon marks the afternoon.

exercises.prompt: It's 12:00 and the sun is directly overhead. Which is the natural way to say it?
exercises.explain: Tanghali is noon/midday, so twelve noon is alas-dose ng tanghali; ng gabi would mean midnight.

exercises.prompt: I am twenty years old. And you, how old are you?
exercises.answer: Dalawampung taon na ako. Ikaw, ilang taon ka na?
accept: Dalawampung taon na ako. Ikaw, ilang taon ka na
Dalawampung taon na po ako. Ikaw po, ilang taon ka na
Dalawampung taon na ako. Ilang taon ka na
exercises.explain: Number + -ng + taon + na states age (dalawampung taon na ako); ilang taon ka na? asks it back.
